coverage.notes: Two weeks of a semester-long lab. Each of the first two labs has a written handout ending in a report checklist, and each has a completed report, so the report format is specified rather than guessed, but later labs (Simulink, hardware) may add requirements that are not here. There is no Week 3 folder. One loose file, Week 3 Lab Report, sits beside the Week 1 and Week 2 folders in OneDrive. It is a hand-algebra draft: two labelled experiments on block-diagram reduction to a transfer function and a step response, with no prose, no report sections, no code, and no sign it was submitted. It shows what one student worked through, not what was required, and it says nothing about the Week 3 report format. Searched by name and by modification date since mid August 2026: all seven iCloud term folders and OneDrive. Found no Week 3 handout, no later report, and no Simulink or toolbox file. File contents were read only for the ENGR 315 lab items, so a handout filed under an unrelated name would be missed. The Lab 1 handout is kept in the iCloud ENGR 315 LAB folder, not in the OneDrive folder. Methods cover MATLAB scripting, the closed-form second-order response, and (provisionally, from that one draft) hand block-diagram reduction; nothing on transfer-function toolbox work, Simulink, or physical-rig measurement. No syllabus was found. MATLAB conventions live in the shared MATLAB tool pack. The host cannot execute MATLAB, so results in a drafted report stay unverified until the student runs the m-file and returns its output.

methods.title: Second-order transient response across damping regimes
methods.when: A lab asks how the damping ratio shapes the free or step response of a mass-spring-damper or any second-order system.
steps: Write the governing ODE from a force balance and name the parameters: M, b, k.
Express the response through the natural frequency and damping ratio, both defined from M, b, k.

Pick one value in each regime the handout lists: undamped, underdamped, critically damped (just below 1 when the closed form divides by sqrt(1 - zeta^2)), overdamped. Choose the underdamped value below 0.5, which the handout says is what lets the damping show.
Compute all cases in one m-file (see the shared MATLAB pack, closed-form-parameter-sweep).

Have the student run it and bring back three things: y(0) for each zeta, which must be 1 in every regime (a check the handout does not require, but the only quick way to catch a sign-flipped overdamped curve); the figure exactly as the script draws it; and every number the analysis will quote.
Tie each regime to its poles, the roots of s^2 + 2 zeta wn s + wn^2: the real part sets decay, the imaginary part sets oscillation.
Check a number with a closed form against the plot, such as the ratio of successive extrema in the underdamped case.

For the underdamped and overdamped regimes the handout says to compare the behavior of different values, while the plot needs only one value each. Make that comparison in the analysis with computed values for a second zeta in each regime, or ask the student whether more traces are wanted.
Explain why the overdamped response is slower than the critically damped one rather than treating it as an error.
pitfalls: The complex branch of acos past zeta = 1, which can flip the sign of the overdamped curve.
Describing the plots without the physics: the checklist asks how M, b, k and zeta produce the behavior.

Reading 'choose one number' as the whole requirement. The handout also says to compare different values within the underdamped and overdamped cases. The archived report compared a second underdamped value in one sentence and no second overdamped value; with no graded copy, whether that met the instructor's expectation is unknown.
Envelope overlays drawn in a line style another curve already uses, which collide in grayscale.
methods.basis: Lab 2 guidelines (experiments and content checklist); the Week 2 submitted report and m-file; the Week 2 output-check notes. The 'compare different values' requirement and the 0.5 bound are the handout's own words, the comparison shortfall is observed in one submission, and the bring-back list is this pack's recommendation.

methods.title: Supporting mathematics
methods.when: Lab 1's math review, and any later lab that needs it.
steps: Partial fractions: factor the denominator, then solve for residues; check by recombining.
Quadratic roots by formula, written as -a +/- b j for complex pairs.
Block reduction to one polynomial numerator over one polynomial denominator: the transfer-function form.
Complex numbers as vectors for sums and differences, and in polar form (magnitude and angle).
Convergence: a decaying exponential reaches steady state; a growing one does not.
pitfalls: Leaving a simplified transfer function with a fraction inside the numerator or denominator.
methods.basis: Lab 1 handout (Experiment 8); the Week 1 submitted report.

methods.title: Block-diagram reduction and step response (provisional)
methods.when: A lab asks for the transfer function of a block diagram with a feedback path, and the response to a step input. The evidence is one student draft of a Week 3 lab and no handout for it was found, so read the lab's own handout first and treat this as a starting point.
steps: Define the transfer function as output over input, T = Y/R, so that Y = T R.

Reduce the loop symbolically first: for negative feedback, the closed-loop transfer function is the forward-path product over one plus the loop product. Name every block before substituting anything, and check the sign at the summing junction.
Substitute the numeric blocks only after the symbolic result is written.
Clear the inner denominators by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by their common denominator, until T is one polynomial over one polynomial.
Spot-check: evaluate the unreduced T and the reduced T at one test value of s that makes no denominator zero. They must agree.
For a step of size A the input is R(s) = A / s. Multiply T by it to get Y(s); the step adds a pole at the origin.
If the handout asks for a plot or a toolbox result, the student runs MATLAB and brings the numbers back. Nothing in this method is evidence about that work.
pitfalls: Turning 1/(1 + a) into 1 + 1/a when simplifying a complex fraction. They are not equal. The draft's numeric reduction did this, and the spot check catches it.
methods.basis: Observed practice in one student draft (a hand-algebra file with two labelled experiments, not known to have been submitted), not a requirement: no handout for the lab was found. The draft does the ordering, the step input and the loop reduction. The spot check is this pack's recommendation. The 1/(1 + a) pitfall is a generic algebra slip that the draft happens to show. The draft says nothing about toolbox work, Simulink, or hardware.

magnitudes.quantity: initial response ratio y(0) / y0, any damping ratio
magnitudes.basis: Handout: an identity of the Lab 2 response equation, not a course convention. With theta = cos^-1(zeta), sin(theta) equals sqrt(1 - zeta^2), so the response starts at y0 in every regime, and the handout sets y0 = 1.
magnitudes.note: The quantity is each curve's first sample divided by y0, so it carries no unit; a raw displacement in mm would not be checked against this range. Exactly -1: that curve came out sign-flipped, because the acos branch used for zeta above 1 disagrees with the sign of sqrt(1 - zeta^2). NaN or Inf: zeta was set to exactly 1. A complex result, or MATLAB's warning about ignored imaginary parts: real() does not cover the whole expression. Any other value: the formula was typed differently from the handout's (theta, the sqrt term, or the exponential).

magnitudes.quantity: ratio of successive extrema, underdamped response, later magnitude over earlier
magnitudes.basis: Handout: the closed form exp(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2)) follows from the handout's response equation, and the range is that value over the handout's advice to choose zeta below 0.5 so the damping shows (0.5 gives 0.163, zeta near 0 gives 1).
magnitudes.note: Above 1: the ratio was taken earlier over later. Below 0.16 is not wrong if zeta was chosen above 0.5: check zeta before questioning the number. About the square of the closed-form value: the two peaks compared were a full period apart, which is a different quantity than successive extrema. Not a course rule; the closed form is the check.
